passage: Priscila sent the message at 7:40 on a Tuesday evening in Porto: 'can I tell you something weird that happened today?' By 8:15 there was nothing, not even the ticks turning blue. She put her phone face down, then picked it up again. Jana always answers. Unless Jana heard what I said at lunch about the dance group. Unless Jana told Marta. Marta tells everyone. By 9:00 Priscila had decided the whole group had a new chat without her and would be polite and cold on Wednesday. She lay on her bed feeling sick, rehearsing how she'd sit alone in the canteen. At 9:42 her phone buzzed. 'sorry!! swimming training ran late and my phone died 😅 tell me!!!'

qa.q: What time did Priscila send her message?
qa.a: Priscila sent the message at 7:40 on a Tuesday evening.

qa.q: Why did each step from 'no reply' to 'a new chat without her' feel certain to Priscila?
qa.a: Priscila was afraid of losing Jana, and the fear filled the silence with the worst meaning; each guess built on the last, so by nine it felt like a known fact.

qa.q: What could Priscila have tried at 8:15 instead of building the story?
qa.a: Priscila could have listed other plain reasons for silence, like training or a dead phone, and done something else for an hour before deciding anything.

qa.q: How might Jana feel on learning Priscila spent two hours sure the friendship was over?
qa.a: Jana would likely feel surprised and a bit sad 😢, having been at swimming training with no idea the silence was being read as anger.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose unanswered message grows, one imagined step at a time, into a lost friendship and a whole group turned against her.

passage: Phone hour in the boys' hostel ended at eight, and Devika still hadn't replied. Wasim had sent her a voice note about the inter-school quiz, the one where he joked that her team would lose. Now he sat in the study hall with his chemistry book open at the same page for forty minutes. She's offended. She's played it to the others. They all think I'm arrogant now. By the time the warden called lights out, Wasim had planned how to avoid the quiz club for the rest of the term. At breakfast the hostel office clerk handed him a folded chit: 'Devika, Class 11B, phoned. Her phone fell in a bucket. Says good luck at the quiz.' Wasim read it three times.

qa.q: Where did Wasim spend forty minutes on the same page?
qa.a: In the study hall, with his chemistry book open at the same page.

qa.q: What was Wasim worried about as he stared at his chemistry book?
qa.a: Wasim worried that his joke had offended Devika, that she had played it to the others, and that they all saw him as arrogant; the silence felt like proof.

qa.q: What choice could have stopped Wasim's spiral before lights out?
qa.a: Wasim could have noticed he had one fact, no reply, and many guesses, and waited for morning or asked Devika directly instead of planning to quit the quiz club.

qa.q: How would Devika likely feel if Wasim had avoided the quiz club all term?
qa.a: Devika would probably be confused and hurt, since the only problem was a phone in a bucket and Devika had even sent good luck.

grounding: Shows a hostel student reading a friend's silence as offence and group scorn, then learning her phone had fallen in a bucket.

passage:
Subject: fine, I get it

Naveen,
It's been two days since I asked if you wanted to go to the cricket trials together. You've been online. I saw. So I'm not stupid. You're done with me. Probably you and Kunal have your own plan for the trials and I'm the extra one. Probably the whole class knows already, which is why Irfan didn't sit with me at lunch. I've gone over it a hundred times and it all fits. So you don't have to pretend on Monday.
Farhan

(Saved in drafts, 11:52 p.m. Not sent. Ammi called me for dinner and asked why my face looked like that, and I said nothing. Maybe I'll read it again tomorrow.)

qa.q: How long had Farhan waited for a reply from Naveen?
qa.a: Farhan had waited two days since asking about going to the cricket trials together.

qa.q: Why does 'it all fits' feel like logic to Farhan?
qa.a: Fear makes Farhan link unrelated things, like where Irfan sat at lunch, into one story; each piece seems to confirm the last, so guesses start to feel like evidence.

qa.q: What could Farhan do before deciding whether to send the email?
qa.a: Farhan could reread it in daylight, separate what is known (no reply, seen online) from what is guessed, and simply ask Naveen about the trials in person on Monday.

qa.q: How might Naveen react if this email arrived with no warning?
qa.a: Naveen might feel accused and confused, since the email blames Naveen for plans and feelings that Farhan has only imagined.

grounding: Shows a teenager turning two days without a reply into a lost friendship and a whole class's judgement, in an email left in drafts.

passage:
Bhaiya, you asked why I was so weird on Saturday. Okay. I'm Nilesh, I'm fifteen, and I'm a bit dramatic. Here's what happened.

I sent Tarun a message at four: "coming for cricket?" Blue ticks. No reply. Five o'clock, nothing. By six I'd worked it out. He's angry because I dropped his catch on Thursday. He's told Imran. Imran's told the whole group. They've made a new chat without me. On Monday nobody will sit with me at lunch.

Each step felt like a fact. I even started deciding where I'd sit alone.

At nine, Tarun called. "Sorry yaar, I read it on the bus and then we went to my nani's village, zero network." That's it. He hadn't even remembered the catch.

What gets me is how sure I was. I didn't know anything. I just had one blue tick and a lot of fear.

qa.q: When did Tarun call Nilesh?
qa.a: At nine, Tarun called.

qa.q: Why did each step feel like a fact to Nilesh, even though it wasn't?
qa.a: Nilesh was scared, and fear filled the silence with the worst explanations, linking them into a chain that seemed logical. The dropped catch gave the story something real to hang on.

qa.q: What could Nilesh try next time a friend goes quiet?
qa.a: Notice the chain as it starts and list other simple reasons for no reply, like travel or no network. Waiting a bit, or sending one light message, is better than planning where to sit alone.

qa.q: How might Tarun have felt if Nilesh had skipped cricket and ignored him on Monday?
qa.a: Tarun would probably have been confused and hurt, since he hadn't even remembered the catch. Nilesh's fear could have created the very distance Nilesh was afraid of.

grounding: A fifteen-year-old tells Bhaiya how one unanswered message led to certainty that a friend was angry and the whole group hated Nilesh, until the friend called.

passage:
I'm Lavanya, Charu's older sister. I'm writing this down because I don't want to forget how fast it happened.

Tuesday after school, Charu, fourteen, sent her best friend Mitali a long voice note about a new song. By dinner there was no reply. Charu kept checking the phone under the table. Amma asked her twice to pass the rasam and she didn't hear.

At nine she came to my room and sat on the floor. "Mitali's ignoring me. She's bored of me. She probably laughed with Keerthi about my voice note. They'll sit together tomorrow and I'll be on my own." She said it like reading the news.

I don't know exactly what was in her head. But her knees were pulled up tight, and she didn't cry, which is worse with Charu.

At 9:40 her phone buzzed. Mitali: "sorry!! tuition ran late, listening now 🎧" Charu laughed, and then looked embarrassed for laughing.

qa.q: What did Amma ask Charu to pass at dinner?
qa.a: Amma asked her twice to pass the rasam.

qa.q: What does Charu saying it "like reading the news" suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: She seemed completely sure that Mitali was bored of her and that she'd be alone, even though nothing had happened yet. The fear felt like fact, not a guess.

qa.q: How could Lavanya help Charu the next time a reply is slow?
qa.a: Lavanya could ask gently what else might explain the silence, like tuition or a flat phone, and suggest waiting a little before deciding anything. Sitting with Charu while she waits also helps.

qa.q: Why is Lavanya unsure what was in Charu's head, and what does she go by?
qa.a: Lavanya can only see the outside: the checking under the table, the tight knees and the lack of tears. Lavanya reads these as signs of fear because she knows Charu well, but can't be certain.

grounding: An older sister watches a fourteen-year-old decide from one slow reply that her friend is bored of her and she will be left alone.
